pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual definition that underpins all percentage work: a percentage is a number of parts PER HUNDRED — a standardised proportion — which is why it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45), why the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts (it is relative to its base, not an absolute quantity), and why percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half times the whole). Standardising 'out of 100' is precisely what makes percentages useful for COMPARING proportions with different totals. Teaching should ground the definition in the 100-grid, hammer the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confront the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.
bestPractices: Define percentage on a 100-grid: shade 45 of 100 cells — 45% = 45/100 = 0.45 = the shaded proportion; the grid makes 'per hundred' literal.
Stress that a percentage is RELATIVE to its whole: 50% of a small quantity and 50% of a large quantity are different amounts — percentage is a proportion, not a fixed number.
Drill the three-way conversion (fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage) in both directions, watching decimal placement (7% = 0.07, not 0.7).
Introduce percentages over 100% deliberately (a 100-grid plus part of a second grid; 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes) so 100% is understood as 'the whole', not a ceiling.
Teach 'express A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, tying it back to proportion (A out of B, restated out of 100).
Use side-by-side comparison tasks (which class did better: 18/25 or 70/100?) so standardising to 'per hundred' is seen to be the point of percentages.
keyRepresentations: 100-grid (each cell = 1%), shaded to show a percentage as a proportion
Two differently-sized bars/quantities with the same percentage shaded (relative-to-whole)
A 100-grid plus a partial second grid to show >100% (150% = 1.5 wholes)
'A out of B, restated out of 100' bridge for expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount (50% is 'the same amount' regardless of the whole), not as a proportion of its base
Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is seen as a maximum rather than 'one whole')
Confuses 'A as a percentage of B' with 'B as a percentage of A', or which quantity is the whole (the base)

learn.summary: A percentage is a number of parts per hundred — a standardised proportion — so it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45). Because a percentage is relative to its whole (base), the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts, and percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half wholes). Standardising 'out of 100' is what makes percentages useful for comparing proportions with different totals. Teaching grounds the definition in a 100-grid, drills the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confronts the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.

activities.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
feedback: If a learner writes 7% = 0.7, point back to the grid: 7 cells out of 100 is 7 hundredths = 0.07; 0.7 would be 70 out of 100 cells.
If a learner thinks the grid cannot be exceeded, give a second grid and ask them to shade 150 cells in total across the two, naming it as one and a half wholes.
Confirm when all three forms (45%, 45/100, 0.45) are matched to the same shaded region.
activities.rationale: Grounding the definition on a 100-grid makes 'per hundred' literal and ties the fraction and decimal forms to a single visible proportion; a second partial grid shows >100% concretely. Curriculum framing treats fractions, decimals and percentages as different ways of expressing proportions.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').

Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid (100 cells, each cell = 1%), shade 45 cells and write the result three ways: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45.
State in your own words what '45 out of 100' means by pointing at the shaded and unshaded parts of the grid.
Shade a second grid partly to show more than one whole: fill one full grid and 50 cells of a second, and write 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes.
Convert a small percentage carefully: shade 7 cells and record 7% = 7/100 = 0.07 (watch that it is 0.07, not 0.7).
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage literally means parts per hundred, so it is the same quantity expressed as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal; 100% is 'one whole', not a ceiling, and percentages can go beyond it.

activities.title: Same percentage, different wholes — 50% of two bags
feedback: If a learner predicts 'the same, because it's 50% of each', have them compute 50% of each whole (10 vs 20) and shade half of each: half of a larger whole is more.

If a learner says 'Bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets', compute both halves — the gap is 10, not 20. The halves differ by 50% of the difference in the wholes; reason from 'half of each', not the raw total gap.
If a learner insists 100% must always beat 50%, return to the trap comparison: 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20, because the percentages sit on different wholes.
Confirm when the learner both gets 'different amounts' AND justifies it by 'half of each whole, and the wholes differ'.
activities.rationale: The percentage-as-absolute misconception is the central error for this topic; predicting then computing and shading the same percentage on two different wholes directly confronts it, and the trap comparison blocks the shortcut '100% always beats 50%' by showing 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. A separate check distinguishes a correct 'no' reasoned proportionally from a 'no' reasoned from the raw total gap.
sourceClaims: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), a peer-reviewed study, documents the percentage-as-absolute misconception: learners treat a percentage as a fixed number added/subtracted regardless of its base — assuming '32% bigger' implies '32% smaller' the other way, and that 32% of one amount equals 32% of a different amount. It states 'a 32% value of one initial amount is not equal to a 32% value of another initial amount — it is important to find out from which whole the percentage is calculated', and that a price +20% then −20% does NOT return to the original.

Per the article abstract (personally fetched), percent is a 'privileged proportion' whose 'extremely concise language has lost its explicit referents, has misleading additive terminology for multiplicative meanings, and has multiple uses for the preposition of', and it 'forms a bridge between real-world situations and mathematical concepts of multiplicative structures' — explaining why learners default to additive schemas. (Abstract verified; full text paywalled.)
learnerActions: Predict first: Bag A has 20 sweets and Bag B has 40 sweets. If you take 50% of each, will you get the same amount from both, or more from one — and why? Write your reason before checking.
Shade half of two bars (or grids) sized to represent 20 and 40, and compare the shaded amounts.
Explain in one sentence why the same percentage gave different amounts.

Check a trap comparison: is 100% of a small 10-sweet bag more or fewer sweets than 50% of Bag B (40 sweets)? Compute both (10 and 20): 50% of the larger bag gives MORE than 100% of the smaller bag — so '100% always beats 50%' is false, because each percentage acts on its own whole.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of its own whole (50% = half of whatever the whole is). Because the wholes differ, equal percentages give different amounts, so a percentage is not a fixed absolute quantity; a larger whole's 50% can even exceed a smaller whole's 100%.

activities.title: Convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage
feedback: If 0.45 is written as 4.5%, re-anchor: 0.45 = 45/100 = 45%; 4.5% would be 0.045.
If 7% is converted to 0.7, re-anchor to 7/100 = 0.07.
Confirm when conversions are correct in both directions, including a value over 100%.
activities.rationale: Fluent two-directional conversion, with attention to decimal placement, is a documented difficulty and a stated curriculum requirement. Recognition/matching is a useful check of whether a learner can identify equivalent forms, but it does not by itself show they can produce a conversion; so matching is paired with learner-produced conversions.
sourceClaims: Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).

Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Match each percentage to its decimal and its fraction-out-of-100 (e.g. 45% ↔ 0.45 ↔ 45/100; 7% ↔ 0.07 ↔ 7/100; 150% ↔ 1.5 ↔ 150/100).
Go in both directions: given 0.08, write the percentage (8%); given 3/100, write the percentage (3%) and decimal (0.03).
Place a given value on a number line that passes 100%, locating 150% at one and a half wholes.
Explain the decimal-placement rule: converting a percent to a decimal divides by 100, moving two places, so a small percent becomes a small decimal (7% → 0.07).
activities.intendedInsight: The three forms are interchangeable notations for the same proportion; converting reliably in both directions depends on tracking the 'out of 100' divisor and decimal place.

activities.title: Express one quantity as a percentage of another, and compare
feedback: If a learner reports 18/25 as the loser without converting, have them compute 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, which beats 70%.
If a learner confuses 'A as a % of B' with 'B as a % of A', mark which quantity is the whole in each phrasing and recompute both.
Confirm when the learner identifies the base correctly and uses A/B × 100.
activities.rationale: Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another and comparing via a common 'out of 100' base are explicit curriculum goals; confusing which quantity is the base is a listed misconception, so direction is checked deliberately.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Write 'A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, and say aloud 'A out of B, restated out of 100'.
Compare two results: one class had 18 out of 25 pass, another 70 out of 100. Convert 18/25 to a percentage (72%) and decide which class did better.
Explain why percentages make this comparison easy: both are restated out of the same total, 100.
Check direction: is 'A as a percentage of B' the same as 'B as a percentage of A'? Try A=10, B=40 (10/40×100 = 25% vs 40/10×100 = 400%) and state which quantity is the whole each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Standardising to 'per hundred' lets you compare proportions with different totals; the base (the 'of B' quantity) is the whole, and swapping A and B changes the question and the answer.

constraints: Keep the base explicit at all times: every percentage is 'of' some whole; when amounts are involved, state the whole before computing.

Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition of equivalent forms but do not, on their own, show the learner can produce conversions or justify the proportional reasoning; pair them with learner-constructed answers and spoken/written explanations.

A static shaded 100-grid is a strong, honest picture of the 'per hundred' definition and the equivalence triple; to let a learner test that the SAME percentage yields different amounts on different wholes, they need to act on at least two different wholes themselves (compute, shade, or physically share), whether with paper grids/bars or an interactive model.

Optional interactive supports — a grid whose fraction and decimal update as cells are shaded, a side-by-side panel shading the same percentage on two differently-sized bars, a drag-past-100% mode onto a second grid, and an 'A as % of B' tool that restates A/B out of 100 — make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same learning can be reached with paper grids, drawn bars, or shared counters.
Distinguish the diagnostic prediction step from the explanation: the reason given BEFORE observing is what reveals the absolute-vs-proportion view.
Do not teach '100% always beats 50%': supply a counterexample, e.g. 100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) is fewer than 50% of a 40-sweet bag (20), so 50% of a larger whole can exceed 100% of a smaller one.
Percentages compare proportions directly because each one is restated out of a common whole of 100. Comparing the actual amounts still needs each whole: 50% of 40 (20) is more than 100% of 10 (10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Scope gap: the objective/evidence includes 'calculate percentage increases and decreases', but no activity builds this (only percentages >100% are represented). The original learn field likewise did not build it, so the rewrite is faithful, but this target is NOT covered and should not be read as taught. The Bassan '+20% then −20%' content is cited for the percentage-as-absolute principle in Activity 2, not for a change-calculation task.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 50% of 20 = 10 and 50% of 40 = 20 (difference 10, not 20); the trap comparison 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20; 18/25 = 72% > 70%; 10/40 = 25% and 40/10 = 400%; 7% = 0.07, 45% = 0.45, 0.45 = 45% (not 4.5%), 150% = 1.5, 0.08 = 8%, 3/100 = 0.03 = 3% — all verified consistent.

Trap-comparison restored to the source form: '100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) vs 50% of Bag B (40) = 10 vs 20', which vividly shows 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. An equal-case variant reusing only Bags A and B (100% of 20 vs 50% of 40 = 20 vs 20) is also mathematically valid and refutes '100% always beats 50%'; reviewers may prefer it for setup economy.

The second misconception ('reaches no by raw total difference') is subtle: the halves differ by 10, which is 50% of the 20-sweet difference in the wholes — preserved in Activity 2 feedback as stated in the source.

The 'conversation/tutor' alternative and the 'per-hundred static grid' explainer from the source are preserved as approaches within activities and constraints rather than as separate ranked artefacts; comparative-efficacy phrasing was softened because the cited sources do not establish one medium as superior.
Source claims are marked 'verified' in the legacy row, but no re-verification occurred here; evidence strength should not be read as freshly confirmed.

assess.poeTask: Show the child two chocolate bars of clearly different sizes — a small one and a large one. Say you will give them 50% of each. PREDICT before breaking anything: will they get the same amount of chocolate from both, or more from one — and WHY? (A child answering 'the same, because it's 50% of each' is treating the percentage as absolute; the reason given before observing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: break each bar in half — the large bar's half is visibly much more chocolate. EXPLAIN: 50% means half of EACH bar's own whole; because the wholes differ, the halves differ — a percentage is a proportion of its base, not a fixed amount.
probeDeeper: 'Write 50% as a fraction and as a decimal' — checks the parts-per-hundred equivalence (1/2, 0.5), and watch for decimal slips.
'Can you ever have more than 100% of something? Give me an example' — surfaces whether 100% is understood as 'the whole' rather than a ceiling.

Counterexample: 'Bag C has 10 sweets — is 100% of bag C more or fewer sweets than 50% of bag B?' — 100% of 10 (=10) equals 50% of 40 (=20)? No: 10 vs 20 — a child who reasons proportionally computes both; an absolute-view child assumes 100% always beats 50%.
'In one class 18 out of 25 passed; in another 70 out of 100 passed — which did better, and why are percentages useful here?' — tests standardising to 'per hundred' for comparison.
assess.correctAnswer: No. 50% of bag A is 10 sweets and 50% of bag B is 20 sweets. A percentage is a proportion of its OWN whole (50% means half of whatever the whole is), so because the bags have different totals, the same percentage gives different amounts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Percentage-as-absolute: 'Yes, 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag' — treats the percentage as a fixed amount, not a proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the two bags: compute 50% of each (10 and 20) and shade half of each on a grid; a percentage is half of ITS whole, and the wholes differ. Rebuild percentage as a proportion of the base.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'yes, the same', or computes only one bag and assumes it holds for both; the percentage is treated as an absolute quantity

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 'no' by the raw difference in totals rather than by proportion: 'bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute both halves (10 and 20, a gap of 10, not 20): the percentage acts on each whole, so the difference in the results is 50% of the difference in the wholes. Anchor to 'half of each'.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — bag B gives 20 more sweets, because it has 20 more sweets than bag A
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the halves differ by 20 (the difference in the bags) instead of 10; reasons from the absolute gap, not 50% of each whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is a maximum, so 150% is impossible or meaningless)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 100% = one whole (the full grid); 150% = one and a half wholes on a grid-plus-half-grid. Percentages describe proportions that can exceed the whole (e.g. prices rising to 150% of the original).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (probe) about 150%, child says 'you can't have more than 100%' or caps it at 100

responseLevels.gap: Treats a percentage as a fixed amount ('50% is the same in both'), or insists percentages cannot exceed 100%; cannot connect percentage to a fraction/decimal of the whole.
responseLevels.full: Defines percentage as parts per hundred / a proportion of its whole, so equal percentages of different wholes give different amounts; converts fluently among fraction, decimal and percentage; interprets and uses percentages greater than 100%; and standardises 'out of 100' to compare proportions with different totals.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises the amounts differ and can compute 50% of each for the practised case, but explains it by the raw difference in totals rather than 'a proportion of each whole', or is shaky on ↔fraction/decimal conversion or on percentages over 100%.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Bag A has 20 sweets and bag B has 40 sweets. Is 50% of bag A the same amount of sweets as 50% of bag B? And — this is the important part — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The prompt forces the relative-vs-absolute distinction and, via the second tier, the REASON. A child who understands percentage as a proportion of the whole says 'no' and explains it by the different wholes; a child holding the absolute view says 'yes, 50% is 50%'. Crucially the tier-two reason also separates a child who reaches 'no' for the RIGHT reason (proportion of each whole) from one who reaches 'no' for a wrong reason (e.g. 'B has 20 more sweets so its half is 20 more') — hard to answer correctly without the proportional idea.
